lede: **24 spellings** of this surname have been put to one record set — FindMyPast's **England Births & Baptisms 1538-1975** — searched nationally, every form asked the same way, every entry of every productive form read. **19 return something. Together they hold 371 baptisms between 1565 and 1909**, and the shape they make is not the shape this archive had assumed.
set: One record set, one county mostly, one index. The set is the FamilySearch transcription of English parish registers and bishops' transcripts, and it is neither complete nor free of duplication — this page counts index entries, not children. Its value here is that it names **the father's first name** for almost every entry, and that the same query can be run fifteen times with only the surname changed. That makes it a measuring instrument for spellings, which is a different job from finding a person.

oneHead: The rarest spelling of all is the one this family used
one: **SANIGOR returns four entries in four hundred and thirty-seven years.** One is Hannah, baptised at Berkeley on 18 August 1804, father Jno. Two more are her family's, Berkeley 1690 and 1691, father Edward. The fourth is a Worcestershire stray. Against 158 SANIGERs and 56 SANIGARs, that is **one entry in eighty-five**. This archive searched for her twice and declared her missing twice, and the reason is on this table: the form the Berkeley clerk used for her is the one no alias list would think to carry.
gapHead: A forty-four-year hole that was never a hole
gap: Read alone, SANIGER at Berkeley has a gap from **1632 to 1676** — forty-four years in which the surname appears not once, which any honest reading would put down to the Civil War and the Commonwealth registers. It is not a gap. **SAINGER supplies twenty-six Berkeley baptisms between 1655 and 1694**, and SANIGOR two more in 1690 and 1691, all of them inside it. For four decades the Berkeley clerk simply wrote the name a different way, and the modern index faithfully preserved his habit as a silence.
twoHead: Two spellings, two places, eight miles apart
two: The forms split cleanly, and the split is geographic. The **-ANIG-** family — SANIGER, SANIGAR, SAINGER, SANIGOR, SANNIGER — belongs to the **Severn Vale**: Berkeley, Thornbury, Stone, Slimbridge, Frampton. The **-INEG-** family — SINEGAR, SINNEGAR, SINNEGER, SINNIGER — belongs to the **Cotswold scarp** above it: Dursley, Cam, Stinchcombe, North Nibley, Alderley. Each has its own patriarchs. In the Vale they are Edward, William and Morgan; on the scarp they are **Abraham at Dursley** from 1698 and **Daniel at Cam** from 1729, and the two sets of names barely touch. The oldest entries of all, SYNIGAR at **King's Stanley in 1591-96** to a William, sit further up the same scarp — and King's Stanley is one of the places the 1608 muster puts this surname.
crossHead: And Hannah's family crossed the line
cross: She was baptised **SANIGOR at Berkeley**, a Vale spelling in a Vale parish. By 1841 she is keeping house in Bristol as **SINEGAR** with a seventy-year-old Lyddya Sinegar, and her brother is **Thomas Sinegar** of St Philip and Jacob, whose children are indexed here as **Lydia Sanigar 1831**, **Ada Sinager 1855** and **John Sinegar 1860**. One family, four spellings, in one city, inside thirty years. Whatever kept the two forms apart in the countryside did not survive the move.
notHead: Two groups that are probably not this name at all
not: **Mortlake, Surrey** holds nine of the ten SYNAGERs and one SINNEGER between 1668 and 1718 — a self-contained family two counties away with no Gloucestershire connection on any record here. And **Whitechapel in 1845 and 1847** has Peter and Johannes Christian Sainger, sons of Cornelius: those are German given names, and SÄNGER is an ordinary German surname. Counting either group into this family would inflate it with strangers.
limits: It is not a count of people. **Thirty-three of the 158 SANIGER entries are duplicates** — 125 distinct name-year-place combinations — and the duplication runs through every spelling: Mary, daughter of Samuell, is indexed four times in 1688, and Sarah, daughter of William, four times at Bristol in 1839. It is not a count of baptisms either, because the set transcribes some registers and not others. It is a count of **what one index holds under fifteen strings**, which is the only thing it can honestly be, and its use is to tell this archive which strings it must ask every future question in.

scarp.head: The other family, on the scarp
scarp.lede: The spelling sweep turned up a second group this archive had never written about, and it is not a footnote: **the -INEG- forms belong to their own parishes and their own patriarchs**, eight miles east of Berkeley and up the hill. They are set out here because leaving them in a table was how they stayed invisible.

scarp.twoHead: Two Solomons, two Deborahs, and what that means
scarp.two: **Daniel of Cam baptised a Solomon in 1745 and another in 1747**, and **Thomas of Cam a Deborah in 1780 and another in 1788**. Repeating a name is what a family did when the first child died, so each pair is almost certainly a burial this archive has not looked for. **Daniel's twelve entries across thirty-one years are the largest single sibling group the surname produces anywhere**, in either spelling family.
scarp.joinHead: Whether they are one family with the Vale
scarp.join: **Not answered, and a baptism index cannot answer it.** The Vale patriarchs are Edward, William, Maurice and Morgan; the scarp's are Abraham, Daniel, John, Thomas and Benjamin, and the two sets of forenames barely overlap. The oldest entries of all — SYNIGAR at **King's Stanley in 1591–96** — sit further up the same scarp, and **King's Stanley is one of the places the 1608 muster puts this surname**. That is the only thread joining the two, and it is a place-name, not a person.
scarp.whyHead: Why it matters to this archive and not only to that one
scarp.why: Hannah Saniger was baptised **SANIGOR at Berkeley**, a Vale form in a Vale parish, and by 1841 she was keeping house in Bristol as **SINEGAR** — a scarp form. Her brother is **Thomas Sinegar** of St Philip and Jacob. **Whoever was writing their surname in Bristol was using the other family's spelling**, and until this sweep this archive had no idea there was another family to borrow it from.

completedHead: A note on the number, which has moved once
completed: This page first reported **340 baptisms across fifteen spellings, twelve of them productive**, on 17 September. That was accurate for the fifteen forms then tried. On **21 September** the remaining forms from this archive's own spelling table were put through the same query, bringing it to 24 tried and 371 baptisms. **The basis did not change and neither did any earlier count** — SANIGER is still 158, SANIGOR still 4. Only the number of questions asked changed, which is the only honest reason a total should move.
exclude: **SINGER and SANGER.** They are in this archive's alias list and they return **127 and 40 in Gloucestershire alone** — because they are ordinary English surnames in their own right, not forms of this one. Counting them would drown the table in strangers, which is the opposite of what it is for.
